title: Britons want open disagreement but lack trusted spaces and confidence to practice it
source_unit: More in Common and University College London, Disagreeing Well research
geography: Britain, with polling and focus-group evidence on political disagreement, identity conflict and civic forums

observations.period: 2026 report; current British attitudes toward expressing disagreement

reluctance_to_speak.unit: per cent saying they are at least sometimes reluctant to say what they really think; 21 per cent say often

negative_label_anxiety.unit: per cent at least sometimes worrying about being labelled negatively when expressing an opinion

silence_reasons.value: The most common reasons for holding back are avoiding an argument (34%), fear of being misrepresented or misunderstood (32%), discomfort (27%) and concern about appearing prejudiced (25%).

youth_label_anxiety.value: Negative-label concern reaches 55% among 18-24 year olds and 54% among 25-34 year olds.

observations.method: More in Common polling combined with focus-group research conducted for the UCL Disagreeing Well campaign; public page does not disclose the full poll sample frame or weighting details.
observations.uncertainty: Reluctance to speak is a self-report and does not measure actual silence, moderation, harassment or political exclusion; focus-group narratives illustrate mechanisms but do not establish prevalence.
observations.subgroup: British adults, with age and party-voter differences in perceived difficulty and fear of negative labels.
observations.counterinterpretation: Holding back can sometimes be a norm of civility or self-protection rather than democratic withdrawal; people may express views in private, at home or through voting instead of public debate.

observations.period: 2026 report; desired norms for political disagreement

debate_every_topic.unit: per cent saying it is important to discuss every topic no matter how strongly people disagree

hostile_disagreement.unit: per cent saying political disagreement in Britain usually ends up hostile or unpleasant

understanding_over_conversion.value: 32 per cent say the most important goal in a political argument is understanding the other person's point of view, compared with 4 per cent who prioritize changing the person's mind.

agree_to_disagree.unit: per cent saying it is often good to agree to disagree if it ends the argument

observations.method: Public polling and focus groups on disagreement norms, goals and skills.
observations.uncertainty: Normative support for listening and open debate does not show that people behave that way in conflict or that respectful disagreement changes political beliefs or policy outcomes.
observations.subgroup: British adults across political parties and generations, with disagreement framed as a learnable civic and interpersonal skill.
observations.counterinterpretation: A preference for understanding may coexist with strong identity boundaries; ‘agree to disagree’ can preserve relationships but also leave unequal power or misinformation unchallenged.

observations.period: 2026 report; civic forums and everyday locations for disagreement

politician_disrespect.unit: per cent saying politicians tend to be rude and disrespectful when debating each other

political_social_media_nonuse.unit: per cent saying they never argue about politics on social media

formal_forum_nonuse.value: 70 per cent never debate politics at college, university or school, and 69 per cent never do so at a local community group or town-hall meeting.

pub_as_space.unit: per cent arguing about politics at the pub at least sometimes, higher than college/school (18%), community or town-hall groups (17%) or in public with strangers (15%)

observations.method: Polling and focus-group research comparing perceived quality and use of Parliament, social media, education, civic groups, town halls and informal social spaces.
observations.uncertainty: Reported venue use is not a complete measure of civic participation; pub participation may be socially selective, and perceptions of politicians may reflect media exposure more than direct observation.
observations.subgroup: British adults using or avoiding online, institutional and informal settings for political discussion.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low use of formal forums may reflect limited opportunity or scheduling rather than rejection; online avoidance can coexist with political learning, private group discussion and other forms of action.

observations.period: 2026 report; perceived social division and political variation

division_perception.unit: per cent saying the UK feels divided, compared with 15 per cent saying it feels united

difficulty_trend.unit: per cent saying it is becoming harder to disagree about difficult topics, compared with 6 per cent saying easier

party_range.value: The view that disagreement is becoming harder spans party groups: 69% among Reform voters, 67% Conservative, 56% Labour, 55% Liberal Democrat and 52% Green voters.

generational_range.value: 74% of 65-74 year olds say disagreement is becoming harder, compared with 45% of 25-34 year olds.

observations.method: More in Common polling and focus groups, with political-voter and age comparisons reported on the public research page.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived division and trend judgments are not measures of objective polarization, social-network segregation or actual cross-group contact; party and age differences may reflect different media environments and issue priorities.
observations.subgroup: British adults by party vote and age, including voters across government and insurgent parties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Recognizing conflict can coexist with resilient pluralism; disagreement may become more visible because more groups and identities are publicly contesting norms.

related_sources.claim: UCL public description of the Disagreeing Well campaign and its focus on constructive debate and listening.
More in Common public research organization and social-cohesion research context.

boundary: This record adds a civic-culture layer: people may value disagreement and understanding while withholding views, avoiding difficult topics and lacking trusted spaces in which to practice political conversation. It is a Britain-focused polling and focus-group synthesis with incomplete public sample details, not a representative longitudinal panel, behavioral trace, causal polarization study or proof that new forums would improve democratic outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official More in Common Disagreeing Well research page was reviewed for public polling and focus-group findings on reluctance to speak, negative labeling, disagreement norms, argument goals, venue use, perceived division, party-voter differences and age differences.
